1:
Delitzsch sets the chapter against the earlier failure: Saul had already transgressed the commandment given through Samuel by the sacrifice at Gilgal, and had drawn on himself the threat that his monarchy should not continue, so that his disobedience here was followed by his rejection. Henry reads the commission as a deliberate test, and says that making this so expressly the trial of his obedience aggravated his disobedience; he hears in the reminder of the anointing an argument from gratitude, since preferment, instead of releasing men from obedience, obliges them so much the more to it. Gill notes that blotting out the name of Amalek was reckoned one of the three things Israel was bound to do on entering the land, and that this work was reserved for their first king; the Hebrew for utterly destroy, Ellicott adds, is stronger, to put under the ban, and what was so devoted could not be redeemed but must be slain.

How so sweeping a sentence is to be justified they answer four ways. Clarke rests the whole weight on authority: nothing could justify such an exterminating decree but the absolute authority of God, and this was given; all the reasons of it we do not know, but we know well that the Judge of all the earth does right. Ellicott refuses the question itself, holding it vain to attempt in such transactions to find materials for the blame or the praise of Israel, which stood in a peculiar relation to the unseen King and was used as the visible scourge by which the All-Wise punished hopelessly hardened sinners. Wesley argues it out instead, that the sentence was not unjust because God is the supreme Lord of life and can require his own when he pleases, that infants are born in sin and so liable to wrath, that their death was rather a mercy than a curse as preventing their sin, and that the beasts, made for man's benefit, may suffer with him. Delitzsch grounds it in the divine nature: when God looks upon a sin, directing his glance towards it, he must punish it according to his own holiness.

Smaller questions divide them. On the muster Clarke surveys the witnesses, the Greek giving four hundred thousand companies of Israel and thirty thousand of Judah, one codex ten thousand of each, another edition two hundred thousand and ten thousand, while the other versions agree with the Hebrew. Henry and Ellicott both find Judah's ten thousand out of proportion to the rest, Henry adding that Judah's day of honour drew near but had not yet come. Delitzsch defends the total instead, since a powerful Bedouin nation could not be attacked with a small army but only by raising the whole military force of Israel. On the place of muster Henry prefers the old versions, which have Saul number them like lambs, or by the paschal lambs, ten men to a lamb.

Why Saul spared what he spared is agreed in substance. Henry assigns two motives, that he spared Agag as a king like himself and perhaps in hope of a ransom, and the cattle out of covetousness, destroying only the refuse that was good for little, which was to honour himself more than God. Ellicott agrees about the covetousness but makes the sparing of Agag a matter of pride, that the king might show the people his royal captive, and Gill offers the same, adding the comeliness of Agag's person. Wesley reduces it to a rule: they obeyed God only so far as they could without inconvenience to themselves. On the escape of the remnant Henry and Delitzsch agree against the letter of the text, Henry supposing that many escaped with their effects into other countries, which could not be helped, and Delitzsch that it follows from the nature of the case, so that there is nothing striking in Amalekites appearing again later.
10:
That God should repent they all take care to qualify, and no two put it quite alike. Henry says repentance in God is not, as in us, a change of mind but a change of method, so that he does not alter his will but wills an alteration, the change being in Saul. Gill says the same and adds that though he repented of making Saul king he never repents of the gifts of his grace. Wesley argues from the term, that repentance implies grief of heart and change of counsels and so cannot be in God, but is ascribed to him when he alters his method and treats a man as if he repented of the kindness shown him. Delitzsch grounds the qualification in the text, that the words express no changeableness in the divine nature but the sorrow of divine love at the rebellion of sinners. Of Samuel's grief Henry observes that he cried to God all night and was not secretly pleased, as many would have been, that his successor was so soon laid aside; Ellicott quotes an earlier expositor for a weightier reason, that Samuel feared the dishonour to God's name if the king God had chosen were cast off.

On the monument they agree about the word, differ about the thing. Ellicott notes the Hebrew is literally a hand, compares the pillar elsewhere so called, and suggests such cairns may have had a hand engraved on them; Clarke thinks it no more than a hand pointing out where the victory was gained; Wesley calls it a trophy; Henry reads it as seeking his own honour more than God's. The conviction by the cattle they relish. Henry says Samuel needed not go far to disprove the profession, the noise the cattle made being a witness against him; Ellicott quotes a commentator for the tone, that citing the animals against him has an air of holy humour and cutting irony. Gill puts the logic plainly: had Saul obeyed, no sheep could have been there to be heard.

The shifting of blame they press differently. Gill compares Saul to Adam laying the blame on his wife. Ellicott finds something strangely cowardly in the transfer, unlike Saul's old character, but adds that covetousness and vanity invariably lead to moral cowardice. Clarke grants that the people very likely did spare the best of the prey, but adds that it is as likely Saul might have restrained them if he would, God having interdicted spoil so that the war might be undertaken from duty alone.

On the great saying they divide in the grounds. Henry distinguishes the two laws: obedience is enjoined by the eternal law of nature and sacrifice only by a positive law, obedience being the law of innocency while sacrifice supposes sin already come into the world and is but a feeble attempt to take away what obedience would have prevented. Wesley makes the same distinction as moral against ceremonial, sacrifice being sometimes unnecessary and sometimes sinful. The last verse Clarke will not read as the others do. The received rendering, he says, is no translation of those difficult words, and the versions all differ; he takes the three nouns of the first half to answer each to the three of the second, transgression to iniquity, divination to the images used in incantation, and rebellion to stubbornness, so that the sense is that as each of these comes of the other, so, because Saul rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord rejected him. Ellicott keeps the plain equation, disobedience in God's chosen king setting aside the true Master of Israel and acknowledging another; Henry says it is as bad to set up other gods as to live in disobedience to the true God, and marks that this is not the rebellion of a people against their prince but of a prince against God.
24:
Whether Saul's confession was sincere is the chapter's sharpest division. Henry says it is too evident that he only acts the part of a penitent, and gives three signs: he applied to Samuel only, confessing that he had transgressed Samuel's word, as if the prophet stood in God's stead, where David said that against God only had he sinned; he excused his fault in the act of confessing it, which is never the fashion of a true penitent; and all his care was to save his credit, so that the words, I have sinned, yet honour me, are the contrary of a penitent's. Gill agrees that the confession was made chiefly to get the sentence reversed, and that the second, though without the first's excuse, appears from what follows to be hypocritical. Wesley contradicts them flatly: it does by no means appear that Saul acts the hypocrite in assigning this cause, but rather he nakedly declares the thing as it was; nor can hypocrisy be proved in the request for pardon, charity requiring us to believe he sincerely desired it of God and man alike. Clarke leans the same way and extenuates, that the people did insist on preserving the best of the prey, and who could resist a victorious mob, though Saul's crime was in consenting. Ellicott takes a middle course, allowing that Saul was terribly in earnest and in great fear, but holding the earnestness founded on a desire to keep his power, and quoting a father: a true penitent would have prayed to be humble rather than honoured.

On the torn garment two questions arise. Delitzsch defends the Hebrew, that the verb is passive and the lappet was torn off rather than torn by Saul, against a proposed correction from the Greek, and holds that it tore accidentally, without any such intention, while Saul was trying to hold the prophet back by force. Ellicott reads it the other way, as a passionate action indicating a restless mind, Saul laying hold of the old man perhaps with some violence; and he corrects the English, since what was seized was not the mantle but the hem of the ordinary tunic worn by the upper classes, the prophetic mantle proper being, he reports, not yet in use in Samuel's day.

The title given to God in the sentence they render variously. Ellicott holds the Hebrew, which occurs first here, would be better rendered the Changeless One of Israel, and that those who give it as the Victory or Triumph of Israel are less accurate; Henry collects the readings without choosing. Wesley takes the title as supplying the reason why God neither will nor can lie, since lying proceeds from a sense of weakness in one who cannot otherwise accomplish his design, whereas God can do whatever he pleases by absolute power.

Why Samuel at last turned back, having just refused, is answered by all and defended by two. Henry supposes he did it on further thoughts and probably by divine direction, to prevent a mutiny or to do justice on Agag, and notes that though Saul worshipped it is not said that Samuel presided. Ellicott gives the political motive, that the prophet's known disapproval and refusal would have been a signal to discontented spirits to revolt under the pretext that it would please the seer. Wesley gives both reasons, that the people might not withdraw their obedience and be as sheep without a shepherd, and that Samuel might execute the judgment Saul had neglected. Both Wesley and Gill defend the change from the charge of falsehood, Wesley holding it no lie because Samuel spoke what he meant and afterwards saw reason to change, which he thinks may relieve many perplexed consciences, and Gill that a good man may change his mind without imputation of a lie.
32:
How Agag came is read three ways from one Hebrew word. Clarke reports the Greek giving trembling and the Hebrew delicacies, a man of delights, while the Latin has him very fat and trembling. Henry offers a choice of senses, that he came in a stately manner to show he was a king, or softly as one never used to hardship, or else so as to move compassion. Delitzsch takes it of his mind rather than his gait, a contented and joyous state, since he thought his life was to be granted him, not having been killed at once. His words are disputed too. Clarke notes that almost all the versions render them differently from the English, giving the sense that death is bitter, which he thinks the true meaning. Henry keeps both senses, that there is bitterness in death and that many think it past when it is not so, putting far from them an evil day which is very near.

Who executed the sentence, and by what right, divides them. Henry reports that some hold Samuel only ordered it done, but thinks he perhaps did it with his own hands, as a sacrifice to God's injured justice, sacrifices being wont to be cut in pieces; and it was done, he adds, by such direction from heaven as none now can pretend to. Clarke makes it magisterial, and thinks it not likely Samuel used his own sword but an executioner's, since what magistrates do officially by their servants they are said to do themselves. Wesley grounds it in the command, that Samuel acted by divine instinct and in pursuance of God's express order, which Saul had neglected and the prophet now executed, but warns that these are no precedents for private persons to take the sword. Ellicott attends to the manner, reporting a suggestion that the words describe a particular form of execution, like the quartering of the Middle Ages. On why Saul had spared him, Ellicott repeats a suggestion he calls curious but not wholly improbable, that kings must spare each other for the honour of their craft; and he offers a theodicy of his own, that the doom of Amalek may have been sent in mercy rather than punishment, mercy to those their evil lives might have corrupted and to themselves, in calling them off from greater evils to come.

That Agag died for his own sins and not his fathers' only they are agreed. Henry says Samuel called him to account not only for his ancestors' sins but for his own, since he trod in the steps of their cruelty. Wesley makes the clause a fuller vindication of God's justice, that although the crime revenged was four hundred years old, God did not punish an innocent son for his father's crimes but one persisting in the same courses. Gill adds that he was a cruel prince who died justly for his own barbarity as well as his ancestors' sins. On the parting all agree, each explaining it differently. Clarke grants that Saul afterwards went to Samuel, which does not affect the statement, since from this time the prophet had no connection with him and never more acknowledged him as king, though he mourned and prayed for him. Wesley glosses the phrase as visiting in token of respect or seeking counsel from God for him, and notes that the later meeting was Saul's coming to Samuel, and that accidentally; Gill reports a supposition that Samuel may have hidden his face. Henry gives three objects of the mourning, that a man who stood so fair should ruin himself so foolishly, the state of a country Saul might have blessed, and his everlasting state; and he draws the lesson that we must mourn for the rejection of sinners though they do not mourn for themselves, Jerusalem having been secure while Christ wept over it.
